Case report
A 55-year-old woman was hospitalized in 1985 to
evaluate the onset of polyuria and polydipsia following an
influenza-like syndrome. A few days later, she developed

elevated blood glucose level (300 mg%) was detected.
Treatment with insulin and glucocorticoid resolved the
clinical disorders (with the exception of a literalized jerk
nystagmus) and normalized the glucose levels. A few
months later, she complained of severe trunk stiffness with
board-like rigidity of the abdomen; an increased response
to exteroceptive stimuli, characterized by painful muscle
spasms, was noted. No limb rigidity was reported, and gait
was normal. Electromyography revealed continuous
motor-unit activity at rest. Diazepam treatment was effec-
tive in reducing the rigidity. Three years later, the rigidity
had completely disappeared, and she presented hypotonia,
gait ataxia, dysmetria, slurred speech and nystagmus. She
was re-hospitalized and a pancerebellar syndrome was
diagnosed at neurological examination. The autoimmune
insulin-dependent diabetes was confirmed by the detection
of anti-islet cell autoAb (ICA). Moreover the organ-specific
autoAb pattern was consistent with a polyendocrine au-
toimmune patient. Islet-cell autoantibodies (ICA), comple-
ment-fixing islet cell antibodies (CF-ICA), gastric

parietal-cell antibodies (GPCA), thyroid microsomial-frac-
tion antibodies (TMFA), thyroglobulin antibodies (TA),
adrenal cortex antibodies (ACA) were detected with
use of standard laboratory procedures (Scherbaum et
1986). No other immunological abnormalities in the

3. Neuroimmunological investigations
The cerebrospinal tluid (CSF) examination disclosed an
increased IgG intrathecal synthesis (Link IgG index 0.8;
N < 0.7) and oligoclonal bands were detected by poly-
acrylamide gel isoelectrofocusing.
The application of diluted patient serum and CSF to rat
cerebella tissue using immunocytochemical procedures
(Giometto et al., 1994; Moll et al., 1995) showed the
presence of circulating autoAb reactive with cerebella
antigens. Briefly, adult Sprague-Dawley rats were perfused
through the ascending aorta with o~. paraformaldehyde.
Their cerebella hemispheres were dissected out, and stored
in cold fixative for 4 h. Frozen sections (8 pm) were
treated with 0.1YCHZOZand with 0.5Y0trypsin. The slides
were then incubated for 1 h at room temperature (RT) with
serial dilutions of patient serum and CSF, washed 3 times
in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) and incubated with
peroxidase-conjugated rabbit anti-human IgG, IgA, IgM
for 30 min at RT. After further washes, the substrate
reaction was developed with diaminobenzidine tetrahydro-
chloride (0.05Yo) and H ~02 (0.01Yc) in PBS and the
sections were mounted in glycerol gelatine. The patient’s
serum and CSF (end-point dilutions 1:5000 and 1:750,
respectively) stained the axon hillocks of Purkinje cells
and diffuse nerve terminals in the molecular and granular
layers of cerebellum (Fig. la). In the cortex and midbrain
individual nerve terminal on the membrane of neurons
were stained (Fig. lb). This pattern is compatible with
GABAergic neuron terminals in the cerebellum and cortex.
Control sera harboring anti-Yo and anti-Hu autoantibod-
ies showed a clearly different pattern of staining when
applied to cerebella tissue (data not shown). Moreover, no
reactivity was detected when negative control sera from
twenty patients affected by other unrelated neurological
disorders (migraine, cerebrovascular diseases, multiple
sclerosis and sporadic cerebella degeneration) were ap-
plied (Fig. Ic).
For immunoblotting, total homogenates of rat brain
tissue was prepared in a medium containing EDTA (lmM)
and a mixture of protease inhibitors in PBS. Total ho-
mogenate was centrifuged at 10OOgfor 15 min and the
supernatant was separated by sodium dodecylstrlphate gel
electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) according to the method of
Laemmli ( 1970) and transferred to nitrocellulose (Towbin
et al., 1979). Nitrocelltr]ose strips were incubated with
patient’s serum (diluted I: 1000) and CSF (1: 100), and with
sera (diluted I: 1000) from the twenty control patients. For
molecular weight estimation, we used a set of SDS molec-
ular weight markers (MW-SDS-70L, Sigma). On Western
blot, the serum and CSF of our patient recognized a band
of 64 kDa (data not shown). No bands were detected in
control samples.
